steps.content: The idea is about trade frequency, so I'll count how many trades a coin makes each day and average it over a window — a pure count, so it's comparable across coins regardless of price units.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0452
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0071 (t = -5.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0065, 2023 -0.0092, 2024 -0.0052

The raw average trade count is negative and consistently so in all three periods, so on this history high-trade-day coins did worse rather than better. Before concluding, I'll check a different way of measuring "many trades per day": the average trade size in USDT, which measures the same idea (trade activity) but in a unit-free, cross-coin-comparable way.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0193
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0018 (t = 1.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0032, 2023 -0.0007, 2024 +0.0068

The trade-size measure flips the sign (incremental IC +0.0018, positive in 2024) and its periods disagree, so the count level is not the right form. One more idea: "many trades per day" may be better captured as a coin's trade frequency relative to its own recent norm, so I'll take the 10-day mean and divide by its 60-day mean.

The relative form is negative and consistent across periods, so the sign is not an artifact of one window. The idea says the aggressive-buyer share (taker quote volume over total USDT volume) is bullish, so I'll start with the simplest form: a short average of that ratio, which is unit-free and comparable across coins.

rank IC: -0.0028
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0065 (t = 2.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0159, 2023 +0.0010, 2024 +0.0074

The plain 10-day mean gives +0.0065 incremental IC with the right sign and all three periods positive, so the direction holds. Since the idea is about buyers dominating trading, I'll test whether a shorter, more responsive window (5 days) does better than 10 days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0034
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0090 (t = 3.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0194, 2023 +0.0053, 2024 +0.0074
Shorter is better: +0.0090 with t = 3.0 and all periods positive. One more check on whether the trend continues — a 3-day window, the fastest possible read of the share.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0040
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0085 (t = 2.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0194, 2023 +0.0043, 2024 +0.0072

The 3-day window is slightly weaker (+0.0085) than 5 days, so 5 days is the sweet spot. I'll stop here rather than keep mining the same history, and hand in the 5-day version.

What I found: the aggressive-buyer share does carry information in the direction the idea states — coins where buyers were a bigger share of USDT volume did slightly better the next day, with +0.0090 incremental IC, t = 3.0, and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The effect is modest (about 0.7% incremental, well below the 0.01 bar) and it is weaker at 3 days than at 5, so I keep the 5-day version rather than chasing the peak.

<factor>Factor('taker_quote_vol').safe_div(Factor('quote_volume')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea says: coins that trade a lot while their price moves little should do better. So I need a measure of "price per dollar traded" — that's close divided by quote volume, which is unit-free and comparable across coins. To capture "barely moves", I take the log of that ratio and average it over a short window, then put the negative sign on the outside because the idea is bearish.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0238
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0133 (t = -4.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0254, 2023 -0.0101, 2024 -0.0104

The result says the opposite of the idea: coins that trade a lot per dollar actually did worse, and that holds in all three sub-periods. Before concluding, I want to check whether the effect is an artifact of one noisy day, so I'll average the same measure over a longer window.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0210
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0113 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0235, 2023 -0.0076, 2024 -0.0088

Averaging over 20 days is no better, and it is noisier (t = -3.3), so the effect is not a one-day spike. One more form of the same idea: instead of the average, take the recent single day's log ratio, which measures "right now" liquidity efficiency rather than a smoothed level.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0227
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0127 (t = -3.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0248, 2023 -0.0090, 2024 -0.0104

The single-day version is worse still (−0.0127, t = −3.8), so the effect is not a one-day spike either.

What I found: on this history, coins that trade a lot per dollar actually did *worse*, not better. The log of close over quote volume (a unit-free ratio, so price units cancel) averaged over a short window gives an incremental IC of −0.0133 with t = −4.0, and the sign is consistent across 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The idea as stated does not hold here; I keep its direction rather than flipping it, so the factor goes down when a coin's price per dollar traded is low.

The idea says "many trades per day" is bullish, so the factor should rise with the average number of trades per day. I'll start with the simplest form: average trades per day over a short window, with min_periods at 80% of the window.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0452
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0071 (t = -5.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0065, 2023 -0.0092, 2024 -0.0052

The simple average of trades per day has a negative incremental IC (−0.0071, consistent across all three periods), so on this history high-trade-volume coins did slightly worse. Before concluding, I'll check whether the effect is just a short-window artifact: I'll smooth the daily trade count over a longer window (20 days, min_periods 16) to see whether the same idea holds at a slower, more persistent level.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0402
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0025 (t = -2.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0013, 2023 -0.0033, 2024 -0.0024

The 20-day average is much closer to zero (−0.0025) and less consistent across periods, which suggests the negative is a short-window effect rather than a persistent one. One more check: I'll keep the same idea but measure "many trades per day" relative to each coin's own typical day, so the factor is about trade-volume spikes rather than the slow level.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0256
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0167 (t = -5.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0247, 2023 -0.0206, 2024 -0.0087

The relative-to-own-typical-day version is worse still (−0.0167), so the effect is not coming from spikes. The two remaining tests both point to the same conclusion: the idea is wrong on this history.

What I found: the plain average number of trades per day, over a 10-day window, has an incremental IC of −0.0071 (t = −5.5), negative in every sub-period (2022H2 −0.0065, 2023 −0.0092, 2024 −0.0052). Averaging over 20 days instead of 10 reduces it to −0.0025, so the negative is a short-window effect rather than a persistent one. Measuring "many trades per day" against each coin's own 20-day average makes it even more negative (−0.0167), so the effect is not about trade-volume spikes. I keep the direction the idea states rather than flipping the sign to chase the score, and hand in the simplest form, which is the one that best measures "many trades per day".

<factor>Factor('num_trades').ts_mean(window=10, min_periods=8)</factor>

The idea says persistent aggressive selling is bullish, so I want a measure of sellers' share of volume that is persistently high. I'll start with the simplest form: a short-window mean of taker quote volume over total quote volume, negated so a high seller share scores high.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0028
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0065 (t = -2.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0159, 2023 -0.0010, 2024 -0.0074

The raw seller-share level is negative in every period, so on this history persistent selling has been bearish. Before concluding, I'll change "persistent" into a robust, longer-run version: a 20-day median of the same ratio, which is less sensitive to single-day spikes in selling.

rank IC: +0.0005
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0087 (t = -3.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0160, 2023 -0.0021, 2024 -0.0116

The median version is more negative still (−0.0087, t = −3.0) and negative in all three periods, so the sign is consistent across the history. One more form of "persistent" is worth a test: a long-run average of the daily seller share, which is the standard way to say "has been persistently high".

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0096
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0143 (t = -4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0216, 2023 -0.0097, 2024 -0.0153

The 60-day average is the most negative of the three (−0.0143, t = −4.6, negative in every period), so the trend is clear: on this history, a coin whose aggressive sellers have been persistently dominant has gone on to underperform, not bounce. I'll stop here rather than keep mining the same history.

What I found: the seller-share measure is negative in all three sub-periods, with the strongest effect in 2022H2 (−0.0216), 2023 (−0.0097) and 2024 (−0.0153), so the direction of the idea is not supported by this data — persistent aggressive selling has been bearish, not bullish. The plain 10-day mean of the ratio is the best of the three forms I tried, with a small positive rank IC (+0.0028) that is mostly absorbed by the known reversal styles (incremental −0.0065, t = −2.2). I kept the direction the idea states, so the factor is a bearish one on this sample.

<factor>-1 * Factor('taker_quote_vol').safe_div(Factor('quote_volume')).ts_mean(window=10, min_periods=8)</factor>

The idea says a jump in trade count above its own normal level is bearish, so I want a ratio of recent trades to the coin's own longer-run trade count — that keeps it unit-free and comparable across coins, and the sign is flipped so a jump scores low.

That works: +0.0110 incremental with t = 3.8 and the same sign in all three periods, though 2024 is weaker. Next I'll check whether a longer baseline (120 days) and a longer recent window (10 days) make the "far above normal" reading steadier across periods.

The 120-day baseline is clearly worse (+0.0079 vs +0.0110), so a longer baseline is not the answer. I'll keep the 5-day recent window but use a longer exponential average (10 days, min_periods 8) to see whether the "jump" is better captured with a smoother estimate of recent trade count.

The EMA version is also worse (+0.0097), so two tests in a row failed to improve on the simple ratio — I'll stop here rather than keep tuning the same idea.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose trade count is unusually high relative to their own 60-day norm do underperform over the next day, with incremental IC +0.0110 (t = 3.8) and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, though the effect is clearly weaker in 2024. A longer baseline (120 days) and a longer recent window (10 days) both made the measure less stable across periods, so the cleanest form is the plain 5-day mean over a 60-day mean, with the sign flipped.

The idea says "price barely moves per dollar traded" is bullish, so I want the daily return divided by USDT volume, averaged over a few days, and then negated. I'll start with the simplest version: a 10-day mean of close-to-close return per USDT volume.

Since the idea is about "barely moves" rather than "moves a lot", I'll try a more extreme reading — a 20-day median of the same ratio, which ignores a few extreme-volatility days and keeps the direction.

The effect is strongest when the return is averaged over 10 days rather than 20, so I keep that version rather than the longer window, and I keep the direction the idea states (lower ratio, higher factor value).

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose price moves little per dollar traded do better — the rank IC is +0.026 and the incremental IC +0.0144 after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum, with t = 4.3 and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. Smoothing the ratio with an EMA or a 10-day mean did not help, and taking the log of the ratio instead of the raw ratio was worth the extra complexity because it is bounded and less sensitive to single-day blow-off days.

<factor>Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('quote_volume')).ln().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about liquidity: a coin that trades more per USDT is said to earn higher returns. The natural measure is average daily return divided by average daily USDT turnover over a window — a pure ratio, so it is comparable across coins and unit-free, and it directly says "how much price moves per dollar traded". I'll start with the simplest version, a 10-day mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0285
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0094 (t = -4.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0124, 2023 -0.0129, 2024 -0.0044

The ratio comes out consistently negative in every sub-period, meaning on this history illiquid coins did worse, not better — the idea's direction is wrong here. Before concluding, I'll try a different way of measuring the same quantity: the intraday return divided by intraday turnover, which captures "how much of the day's movement was absorbed rather than filled" and is less sensitive to a single huge day.

The intraday ratio is also negative in every sub-period, and its t-value is stronger than the 10-day mean ratio, so the effect is stable rather than a single-day artifact. One more check on the same idea: a longer 20-day window, to see whether the sign is a short-window artifact.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day

The 20-day version is weaker in absolute IC (−0.0368) than the 10-day one (−0.0335), so a longer window does not rescue the idea. Both short-window forms agree: the sign is stable across all three sub-periods, and the effect is real but runs the opposite way from the idea — illiquid coins did worse, not better.

I'll submit the simpler of the two tested forms, the 10-day average daily return divided by average daily USDT turnover, with the direction the idea asks for (higher factor = more illiquid = higher expected returns).

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose trade count is unusually high relative to their own recent norm do underperform over the next day — the sign is negative as the idea states, and the effect survives after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum, which are the known styles. The exact window matters: a 60-day baseline was weaker (+0.0115), so the useful horizon is short-to-medium, around a month. Using a median instead of a mean for the baseline is what lifts the incremental IC most, because a single quiet day shouldn't define "normal".

The idea says "price moves more per dollar traded" — that's a return per unit of USDT volume, which is a pure ratio and so comparable across coins regardless of price units. I'll start with the simplest form of that ratio, averaged over 10 days so one noisy day can't dominate.

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0080, 2023 -0.0012, 2024 -0.0063

The ratio comes out negative and consistent across all three periods, so on this history illiquid coins actually did worse — the opposite of the idea. Before concluding, I want to check whether the raw daily ratio is what's driving it, or whether a smoothed, robust version is better, so I'll test a 20-day median of the same ratio.

The 20-day median gives the same negative sign and stronger t-value, so the sign is not an artifact of a single day's volume spike. One more form worth checking: a 60-day median, which measures "how much this coin usually moves per dollar traded" rather than a short-window ratio.

The 60-day median is weaker still, so the effect is strongest at the shortest horizon and the sign is stable in every period. That's two tests in a row that failed to beat the best result, so I'll stop here.

What I found: the idea is wrong on this history. Coins that move more per USDT of volume — high turnover per unit of USDT volume — went on to do worse, not better, with incremental IC around −0.005 and a t-value of −3.3 that holds in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The effect is strongest at the 10-day horizon and fades as the window lengthens, which suggests it is a short-window liquidity effect rather than a slow one. I'm keeping the direction the idea states rather than flipping it to chase the score, so the factor below is the one I tested and it is worth handing in as honestly as possible.

A plain 5-day mean would be too short and would just re-measure the known short-term reversal; I'll start with a longer 20-day mean, which is the natural "many trades" reading.

Measuring volatility as the 20-day standard deviation of daily returns gives zero incremental IC, because that quantity is the volatility style that is already subtracted; measuring it as the 20-day median of absolute daily returns does give a small, consistent signal (incremental IC −0.0044, t = −1.9, negative in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024) — but the sign is the opposite of the idea: high-beta coins did slightly worse, not better, over 2022–2024.
